```{r}
#| label: setup

# Load packages
library(glmmTMB)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom.mixed)
library(performance)
library(gt)
library(readr)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)
library(titanic)

# Load the data
titanic <- titanic_train

# Keep the same complete-case sample for every model
titanic <- titanic |>
  select(Survived, Sex, Age, Pclass) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    Sex.Binary = case_when(
      Sex == "male" ~ 0,
      Sex == "female" ~ 1)) |>
  mutate(
    Survived.Char = case_when(
      Survived == 0 ~ "Died",
      Survived == 1 ~ "Survived")) |>
  mutate(
    Pclass.Char = case_when(
      Pclass == "1" ~ "First Class",
      Pclass == "2" ~ "Second Class",
      Pclass == "3" ~ "Third Class")) |>
  mutate(Pclass = factor(Pclass, levels = c(1, 2, 3))) |>
  select(Survived, Survived.Char, Sex, Sex.Binary, Pclass, Pclass.Char, Age)

n <- nrow(titanic)

# Helper: format a number without a leading zero (e.g., .045)
no0 <- function(x, digits = 3) sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), x))

# Helper: format a p-value for text (e.g., "< .001" or "= .045")
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", no0(p, 3)))
```

# 1. Data and exploration

This analysis uses the `titanic_train` data from the `titanic` package. After keeping passengers with complete data on survival, sex, age, and ticket class, the sample contains `r n` passengers. The outcome is whether a passenger survived the sinking, and the predictors are sex, ticket class (a proxy for socioeconomic status), and age.

## Descriptive statistics

```{r}
#| label: tbl-age
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics for age"

# Mean, SD, min and max for the continuous variable
age_table <- titanic |>
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(Age),
    SD = sd(Age),
    Min = min(Age),
    Max = max(Age)) |>
  mutate(Variable = "Age (years)", .before = 1)

age_table |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Mean, SD, Min, Max), decimals = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-counts
#| tbl-cap: "Cell counts for the categorical variables"

# Cell counts and percentages for each categorical variable
cell_counts <- bind_rows(
  titanic |> count(Level = Survived.Char) |> mutate(Variable = "Survival"),
  titanic |> count(Level = tools::toTitleCase(Sex)) |> mutate(Variable = "Sex"),
  titanic |> count(Level = Pclass.Char) |> mutate(Variable = "Ticket class")) |>
  mutate(Percent = n / nrow(titanic) * 100)

cell_counts |>
  gt(groupname_col = "Variable") |>
  fmt_number(columns = Percent, decimals = 1) |>
  cols_label(Level = "Category", n = "n", Percent = "Percent (%)")
```

```{r}
#| label: exploration-stats

# Values used inline in the exploration paragraph
n_surv   <- sum(titanic$Survived == 1)
pct_surv <- mean(titanic$Survived == 1) * 100
pct_fem  <- mean(titanic$Sex == "female") * 100
pct_c1   <- mean(titanic$Pclass == 1) * 100
pct_c3   <- mean(titanic$Pclass == 3) * 100

# Survival rate within each group
surv_sex <- titanic |> group_by(Sex) |> summarise(p = mean(Survived) * 100)
surv_cls <- titanic |> group_by(Pclass) |> summarise(p = mean(Survived) * 100)
surv_f   <- surv_sex$p[surv_sex$Sex == "female"]
surv_m   <- surv_sex$p[surv_sex$Sex == "male"]
surv_c1  <- surv_cls$p[surv_cls$Pclass == 1]
surv_c3  <- surv_cls$p[surv_cls$Pclass == 3]
```

## Exploratory patterns

Of the `r n` passengers, `r n_surv` (`r round(pct_surv, 1)`%) survived. The sample was not evenly split across the categorical variables. About `r round(pct_fem, 1)`% of passengers were female, and `r round(pct_c3, 1)`% held third-class tickets compared with `r round(pct_c1, 1)`% in first class, so the cell counts are uneven, though every cell is large enough to estimate. Ages averaged `r round(mean(titanic$Age), 1)` years (SD = `r round(sd(titanic$Age), 1)`), ranging from `r round(min(titanic$Age), 2)` to `r round(max(titanic$Age), 0)`. The clearest pattern is that survival differed sharply by group: `r round(surv_f, 1)`% of women survived compared with `r round(surv_m, 1)`% of men, and `r round(surv_c1, 1)`% of first-class passengers survived compared with `r round(surv_c3, 1)`% in third class. These patterns are consistent with my expectations, which are described below.

# 2. Specify competing models

## Predictions

I expected all three predictors to be associated with survival. Given the “women and children first” practice during emergencies at the time of the Titanic sinking, I anticipated that women would have higher odds of survival than men. I also expected ticket class, which I used as an indicator of socioeconomic status, to influence survival. First-class passengers may have had easier access to lifeboats, crew members, and important information, which could have increased their chances of survival compared with third-class passengers. Similarly, I expected younger passengers to have higher odds of survival because children were often prioritized during evacuation. Overall, I anticipated that sex and ticket class would have the strongest associations with survival, while age would make a smaller additional contribution after accounting for the other two predictors.


We will estimate four nested models:

| Model | Predictors | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| mod0: Null | Intercept only | Baseline model |
| mod1: Sex | Sex | Evaluate sex |
| mod2: Sex + Pclass | Sex, Pclass | Additional contribution of ticket class |
| mod3: Sex + Pclass + Age | Sex, Pclass, Age | Additional contribution of age |

```{r}
#| label: fit-models

# Fit the four nested binary logistic regression models
mod0 <- glmmTMB(Survived ~ 1, data = titanic, family = binomial)
mod1 <- glmmTMB(Survived ~ Sex, data = titanic, family = binomial)
mod2 <- glmmTMB(Survived ~ Sex + Pclass, data = titanic, family = binomial)
mod3 <- glmmTMB(Survived ~ Sex + Pclass + Age, data = titanic, family = binomial)

# Intercepts (log-odds) used in the paragraph below
int1 <- fixef(mod1)$cond[["(Intercept)"]]
int2 <- fixef(mod2)$cond[["(Intercept)"]]
int3 <- fixef(mod3)$cond[["(Intercept)"]]
```

## How the intercept changes

The meaning of the intercept changes with each model because it always describes the log-odds of survival when every predictor is at its reference value. In mod1, the intercept (`r no0(int1, 2)`) is the log-odds of survival for a female passenger, since female is the reference level of sex. In mod2, the intercept (`r no0(int2, 2)`) is the log-odds of survival for a female passenger in first class. In mod3, the intercept (`r no0(int3, 2)`) is the log-odds of survival for a female first-class passenger aged 0. Age 0 is just below the youngest passenger in the data (`r round(min(titanic$Age), 2)` years), so this intercept is a baseline for the model and not a typical passenger.

# 3. Compare model performance

```{r}
#| label: comparison-stats

# Nested likelihood-ratio (chi-square) tests, in order mod0 to mod3
tests <- as.data.frame(anova(mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3)) |>
  select(`Chi Df`, Chisq, `Pr(>Chisq)`) |>
  rename(nested_df = `Chi Df`, nested_chisq = Chisq, nested_p = `Pr(>Chisq)`)

# Model-level statistics from glance()
performance_table <- bind_rows(
  glance(mod0), glance(mod1), glance(mod2), glance(mod3)) |>
  mutate(
    Model = c("mod0: Null", "mod1: Sex", "mod2: + Pclass", "mod3: + Age"),
    deviance = -2 * as.numeric(logLik)) |>
  select(Model, AIC, BIC, logLik, deviance, df.residual)

# Combine into one table (same four models in the same order)
comparison_table <- cbind(performance_table, tests)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Model comparison and nested likelihood-ratio tests"

comparison_table |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(AIC, BIC, logLik, deviance, nested_chisq), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt(columns = nested_p,
      fns = function(x) ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "—") |>
  cols_label(
    df.residual = "Residual df",
    nested_df = "Nested df",
    nested_chisq = "Nested χ²",
    nested_p = "Nested p")
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-values

# Pull values from the comparison table so the text updates automatically
aic <- comparison_table$AIC
bic <- comparison_table$BIC
chi <- comparison_table$nested_chisq
pv  <- comparison_table$nested_p
ddf <- comparison_table$nested_df
```

## Interpreting the comparisons

The best-fitting model was mod3 (sex, ticket class, and age), which had the lowest AIC (`r round(aic[4], 1)`) and the lowest BIC (`r round(bic[4], 1)`) of the four models. AIC and BIC both fell with every predictor added. AIC dropped from `r round(aic[1], 1)` in the null model to `r round(aic[2], 1)` with sex, `r round(aic[3], 1)` with ticket class, and `r round(aic[4], 1)` with age. BIC followed the same pattern, falling from `r round(bic[1], 1)` to `r round(bic[2], 1)`, `r round(bic[3], 1)`, and `r round(bic[4], 1)`. The likelihood-ratio tests showed that each addition significantly improved fit: sex improved on the intercept-only model (χ²(`r ddf[2]`) = `r round(chi[2], 2)`, p `r fmt_p(pv[2])`), ticket class improved on sex alone (χ²(`r ddf[3]`) = `r round(chi[3], 2)`, p `r fmt_p(pv[3])`), and age improved on sex and ticket class (χ²(`r ddf[4]`) = `r round(chi[4], 2)`, p `r fmt_p(pv[4])`). AIC, BIC, and the likelihood-ratio tests therefore support the same conclusion. This agreement is expected here, because even the smallest improvement (age) is much larger than the extra penalty that BIC places on one additional parameter, which is the stricter of the two criteria with `r n` passengers. The size of the improvements also shows that the predictors contributed unequally. Sex produced by far the largest gain, ticket class added a substantial improvement beyond sex, and age added the smallest but still clearly significant improvement.

# 4. Evaluate binary logistic regression diagnostics

I examined mod3, the model with the best AIC and BIC and with every likelihood-ratio test significant, as the most promising model.

## Residual diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: dharma-sim

# Simulate scaled (quantile) residuals for the selected model
set.seed(123)
sim <- simulateResiduals(mod3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dharma-qq
#| fig-cap: "DHARMa QQ plot of simulated residuals for mod3"
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4.5

# QQ plot without the on-plot test labels (the tests are reported in the table below)
plotQQunif(sim, testUniformity = FALSE, testDispersion = FALSE, testOutliers = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dharma-pred
#| fig-cap: "DHARMa residuals against model predictions for mod3"
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Residuals against predicted values
plotResiduals(sim)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-resid-age
#| fig-cap: "DHARMa residuals against age"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Is the relationship between age and the logit adequately represented?
plotResiduals(sim, titanic$Age, xlab = "Age")
```

```{r}
#| label: dharma-tests

# Formal DHARMa tests
t_unif <- testUniformity(sim, plot = FALSE)
t_disp <- testDispersion(sim, plot = FALSE)
t_outl <- testOutliers(sim, plot = FALSE)

dharma_table <- data.frame(
  Test = c("Uniformity of residuals (KS)", "Dispersion", "Outliers"),
  Statistic = c(unname(t_unif$statistic), unname(t_disp$statistic), unname(t_outl$statistic)),
  p = c(t_unif$p.value, t_disp$p.value, t_outl$p.value))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dharma
#| tbl-cap: "DHARMa diagnostic tests for mod3"

dharma_table |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = Statistic, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt(columns = p, fns = function(x) ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x)))
```

## Collinearity

```{r}
#| label: tbl-vif
#| tbl-cap: "Variance inflation factors for mod3"

vif_table <- as.data.frame(check_collinearity(mod3))

vif_table |>
  select(Term, VIF, Tolerance) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(VIF, Tolerance), decimals = 2)
```

## Complete separation and events per predictor

```{r}
#| label: tbl-separation
#| tbl-cap: "Survival counts within each sex and ticket-class cell"

# Separation would show up as a cell where everyone survived or everyone died
sep_table <- titanic |>
  group_by(Sex, Pclass) |>
  summarise(
    Passengers = n(),
    Survived = sum(Survived == 1),
    Died = sum(Survived == 0),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(Died = Passengers - Survived)

sep_table |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(Pclass = "Ticket class")
```

```{r}
#| label: epp-stats

# Events per predictor: the smaller outcome group divided by the number of coefficients
n_events    <- min(sum(titanic$Survived == 1), sum(titanic$Survived == 0))
n_coefs     <- length(fixef(mod3)$cond) - 1   # excludes the intercept
epp         <- n_events / n_coefs

# Did the model converge with a well-defined Hessian?
converged   <- mod3$sdr$pdHess
```

## Diagnostic findings

Most assumptions appeared reasonably satisfied. The simulated-residual QQ plot followed the reference line closely, and none of the DHARMa tests detected a problem: uniformity (KS p `r fmt_p(t_unif$p.value)`), dispersion (p `r fmt_p(t_disp$p.value)`), and outliers (p `r fmt_p(t_outl$p.value)`).The DHARMa outlier test also found no more extreme residuals than expected, suggesting that unusual observations were not a major concern. In the plot of residuals against predicted values, the quantile lines curved only slightly, and DHARMa's combined adjusted quantile test was not significant. Collinearity was not a concern, because the largest variance inflation factor was `r round(max(vif_table$VIF), 2)`, well below the usual threshold of 5. There was no sign of complete separation. Every combination of sex and ticket class contained both survivors and non-survivors (the smallest counts were `r min(sep_table$Survived)` survivors and `r min(sep_table$Died)` non-survivors in a cell), and the model converged with a well-defined Hessian. The model had `r n_events` events (the smaller outcome group) for `r n_coefs` coefficients, or `r round(epp, 1)` events per predictor, far above the common guideline of 10.

One potential concern was identified in the plot of residuals against age. DHARMa's combined quantile test was significant, and the smoothed lines showed a wavy pattern, suggesting that the model may not fully capture the relationship between age and survival. This may be because the model assumes a linear relationship between age and the log-odds of survival, which may not adequately reflect differences across age groups, particularly among younger children. Although age significantly improved model fit, its coefficient should be interpreted cautiously because it represents an overall linear trend. The findings for sex and ticket class remain strongly supported under the current model, although modelling age differently could affect their estimates. Overall, I remain reasonably confident in mod3 as the preferred model among those compared, while acknowledging this limitation.


# 5. Select and report the preferred model

## Model selection

```{r}
#| label: selected-model

# The preferred model
selected_model <- mod3
```

I selected mod3 (sex, ticket class, and age) as my preferred model. It had the lowest AIC (`r round(aic[4], 1)`) and BIC (`r round(bic[4], 1)`), and each addition of a predictor produced a statistically significant improvement in the likelihood-ratio tests, including age (χ²(`r ddf[4]`) = `r round(chi[4], 2)`, p `r fmt_p(pv[4])`). Because BIC applies the stronger penalty for complexity and still favoured mod3, the extra parameters are justified. The diagnostics did not show any serious problems with mod3, apart from the mild nonlinearity in the age effect. The model is also easy to interpret, since each predictor corresponds to one of the substantive questions the analysis set out to address (sex, socioeconomic status, and age). I preferred mod3 to mod2 because age improved fit significantly and has a clear substantive meaning, and to mod1 and mod0 because they leave out predictors that clearly improved fit. Mod2 remains a reasonable alternative for a reader who is concerned about the linear form of the age effect.

## Coefficient table

```{r}
#| label: extract-coefficients

# Unstandardized coefficients (log-odds), 95% CIs, and odds ratios
coefficient_results <- tidy(selected_model, effects = "fixed", component = "cond",
                            conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95) |>
  mutate(
    OR = exp(estimate),
    OR_low = exp(conf.low),
    OR_high = exp(conf.high))

# Helper: pull one value for one predictor
coef_val <- function(predictor, column) {
  coefficient_results[coefficient_results$term == predictor, ][[column]]
}

# Readable predictor names
pred_labels <- c(
  "(Intercept)" = "Intercept",
  "Sexmale" = "Sex: male (vs. female)",
  "Pclass2" = "Ticket class: second (vs. first)",
  "Pclass3" = "Ticket class: third (vs. first)",
  "Age" = "Age (per year)")

coefficient_table <- coefficient_results |>
  mutate(Predictor = unname(pred_labels[term])) |>
  select(Predictor, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, p.value, OR, OR_low, OR_high)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coefficients
#| tbl-cap: "Unstandardized logistic regression coefficients (log-odds) and odds ratios for the selected model"

coefficient_table |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, OR, OR_low, OR_high),
             decimals = 3) |>
  fmt(columns = p.value,
      fns = function(x) ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "95% CI (log-odds)", columns = c(conf.low, conf.high)) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Odds ratio", columns = c(OR, OR_low, OR_high)) |>
  cols_label(
    estimate = "Estimate", std.error = "SE",
    conf.low = "Lower", conf.high = "Upper", p.value = "p",
    OR = "OR", OR_low = "Lower", OR_high = "Upper")
```

## Interpreting the coefficients

Sex: Holding ticket class and age constant, the log-odds of survival were `r no0(abs(coef_val("Sexmale", "estimate")), 2)` lower for men than for women, 95% CI [`r no0(coef_val("Sexmale", "conf.low"), 2)`, `r no0(coef_val("Sexmale", "conf.high"), 2)`], p `r fmt_p(coef_val("Sexmale", "p.value"))`. As an odds ratio, the odds of survival for men were `r no0(coef_val("Sexmale", "OR"), 2)` times the odds for women (95% CI [`r no0(coef_val("Sexmale", "OR_low"), 2)`, `r no0(coef_val("Sexmale", "OR_high"), 2)`]), which is a reduction of about `r round((1 - coef_val("Sexmale", "OR")) * 100)`%.

Ticket class: Holding sex and age constant, passengers in second class had log-odds of survival `r no0(abs(coef_val("Pclass2", "estimate")), 2)` lower than passengers in first class, 95% CI [`r no0(coef_val("Pclass2", "conf.low"), 2)`, `r no0(coef_val("Pclass2", "conf.high"), 2)`], p `r fmt_p(coef_val("Pclass2", "p.value"))`, an odds ratio of `r no0(coef_val("Pclass2", "OR"), 2)` (95% CI [`r no0(coef_val("Pclass2", "OR_low"), 2)`, `r no0(coef_val("Pclass2", "OR_high"), 2)`]). Third-class passengers had log-odds of survival `r no0(abs(coef_val("Pclass3", "estimate")), 2)` lower than first-class passengers, 95% CI [`r no0(coef_val("Pclass3", "conf.low"), 2)`, `r no0(coef_val("Pclass3", "conf.high"), 2)`], p `r fmt_p(coef_val("Pclass3", "p.value"))`, an odds ratio of `r no0(coef_val("Pclass3", "OR"), 2)` (95% CI [`r no0(coef_val("Pclass3", "OR_low"), 2)`, `r no0(coef_val("Pclass3", "OR_high"), 2)`]).

Age: Holding sex and ticket class constant, each additional year of age was associated with a `r no0(abs(coef_val("Age", "estimate")), 3)` decrease in the log-odds of survival, 95% CI [`r no0(coef_val("Age", "conf.low"), 3)`, `r no0(coef_val("Age", "conf.high"), 3)`], p `r fmt_p(coef_val("Age", "p.value"))`. The odds ratio of `r no0(coef_val("Age", "OR"), 3)` (95% CI [`r no0(coef_val("Age", "OR_low"), 3)`, `r no0(coef_val("Age", "OR_high"), 3)`]) means that each additional year multiplied the odds of survival by about that amount, or `r no0(coef_val("Age", "OR")^10, 2)` for every ten years.

The intercept is the log-odds of survival (`r no0(coef_val("(Intercept)", "estimate"), 2)`) for a female first-class passenger aged 0, so it serves as a baseline and not as a typical passenger.

## Overall model performance

```{r}
#| label: performance-stats

# Predicted probabilities for the selected model
pred_prob <- predict(selected_model, type = "response")

# Tjur's R-squared: mean predicted probability for survivors minus for non-survivors
tjur_r2 <- mean(pred_prob[titanic$Survived == 1]) - mean(pred_prob[titanic$Survived == 0])

selected_row <- comparison_table[comparison_table$Model == "mod3: + Age", ]

selected_performance <- data.frame(
  Model = "mod3: Sex + Pclass + Age",
  AIC = selected_row$AIC,
  BIC = selected_row$BIC,
  logLik = selected_row$logLik,
  deviance = selected_row$deviance,
  Tjur_R2 = tjur_r2)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Overall performance of the selected model"

selected_performance |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(AIC, BIC, logLik, deviance), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = Tjur_R2, decimals = 3) |>
  cols_label(Tjur_R2 = "Tjur's R²")
```

The selected model had an AIC of `r round(selected_row$AIC, 1)`, a BIC of `r round(selected_row$BIC, 1)`, and a deviance of `r round(selected_row$deviance, 1)` (compared with `r round(comparison_table$deviance[1], 1)` for the null model). Tjur's R² was `r no0(tjur_r2, 3)`, meaning that the model's predicted probability of survival was on average about `r round(tjur_r2 * 100)` percentage points higher for passengers who survived than for those who died. This describes fit to these `r n` passengers, not how well the model would predict survival in new data.

## Summary of results

I examined the association between sex, ticket class (a proxy for socioeconomic status), and age and survival of the Titanic sinking among `r n` passengers, using four nested binary logistic regression models. Likelihood-ratio tests, AIC, and BIC all favoured the model with all three predictors (mod3). In that model, holding the other predictors constant, the odds of survival for men were `r no0(coef_val("Sexmale", "OR"), 2)` times the odds for women (95% CI [`r no0(coef_val("Sexmale", "OR_low"), 2)`, `r no0(coef_val("Sexmale", "OR_high"), 2)`]). The odds of survival for second-class passengers were `r no0(coef_val("Pclass2", "OR"), 2)` times those of first-class passengers (95% CI [`r no0(coef_val("Pclass2", "OR_low"), 2)`, `r no0(coef_val("Pclass2", "OR_high"), 2)`]), and for third-class passengers they were `r no0(coef_val("Pclass3", "OR"), 2)` times those of first-class passengers (95% CI [`r no0(coef_val("Pclass3", "OR_low"), 2)`, `r no0(coef_val("Pclass3", "OR_high"), 2)`]). Each additional year of age multiplied the odds of survival by `r no0(coef_val("Age", "OR"), 3)` (95% CI [`r no0(coef_val("Age", "OR_low"), 3)`, `r no0(coef_val("Age", "OR_high"), 3)`]). Diagnostics supported the model overall, with one caveat about the linearity of the age effect.

## Visualizing age

```{r}
#| label: fig-age-effect
#| fig-cap: "Predicted probability of survival by age, for a female first-class passenger (shaded band = 95% CI)"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Adjusted predictions for age from the selected model
age_pred <- ggpredict(selected_model, terms = "Age")

ggplot(age_pred, aes(x = x, y = predicted)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), fill = "grey80") +
  geom_line(color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Predicted probability of survival") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 13)
```

# 6. Discussion and limitations

Sex was the most important predictor of survival, followed by ticket class, and then age. Adding sex to the null model produced the largest improvement in fit (χ²(`r ddf[2]`) = `r round(chi[2], 1)`), ticket class added a substantial improvement beyond sex (χ²(`r ddf[3]`) = `r round(chi[3], 1)`), and age added the smallest improvement (χ²(`r ddf[4]`) = `r round(chi[4], 1)`), although all three were statistically significant. The odds ratios show the same ordering. Men had far lower odds of survival than women (OR = `r no0(coef_val("Sexmale", "OR"), 2)`), third-class passengers had far lower odds than first-class passengers (OR = `r no0(coef_val("Pclass3", "OR"), 2)`), and each additional year of age reduced the odds only modestly (OR = `r no0(coef_val("Age", "OR"), 3)` per year). These results fit the historical account that women, first-class passengers, and children were prioritized in the evacuation, and they suggest that gender norms and social class both shaped who survived.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, the data are observational and come from a single historical event, meaning that the results demonstrate associations rather than causal relationships. Second, the analysis included only 714 passengers with complete data, excluding 177 passengers with missing age information. This may limit how well the findings represent all passengers in the original dataset. Third, ticket class was used as an indicator of socioeconomic status, but it may not fully capture differences in wealth or other factors, such as cabin location, that could have influenced survival. Another limitation concerns age, as the diagnostic results suggested that its relationship with the log-odds of survival may not be entirely linear. Therefore, the age coefficient should be interpreted cautiously because it may not fully capture differences in survival across age groups, particularly among younger children. Additionally, the models did not examine possible interactions between predictors. For example, the relationship between sex and survival may have differed across ticket classes. Finally, the model performance was evaluated using the same passengers included in the analysis, so the results do not necessarily reflect how well the model would perform on new data.
